title: Complexity of Differentially Private Selection via Federated APIs
gist: A NeurIPS paper from Apple ML Research (Asi, Feldman, Nelson, Nguyen, Talwar, Zhou) proves that differentially private selection built on the standard noisy secure-aggregation primitive needs on the order of sqrt(d)/epsilon samples, and proposes adding a Sparse Vector Technique (SVT) primitive to federated APIs that matches central-model error with near-optimal query counts, giving an exponential separation from shuffle and aggregation models.

insights.claim: In federated or distributed settings, differential privacy implementations built on local, shuffle and secure-aggregation models suffer a significant utility gap versus the central DP model, incurring high error on tasks such as selection.
insights.speaker: Apple ML Research
insights.so_what: On-device analytics built purely on aggregation primitives (as in federated telemetry) structurally pay an accuracy tax versus server-side analytics.

insights.so_what: Better engineering of existing aggregation APIs cannot close the gap; the API surface itself has to change.

insights.speaker: Apple ML Research
insights.so_what: Signals a possible future building block for Apple-style private federated analytics infrastructure beyond secure aggregation.

insights.claim: With the SVT primitive, an epsilon-differentially private selection algorithm in dimension d achieves additive error O(log(dn)/epsilon), matching the central model when n is polynomially bounded in d, using a near-optimal expected O(d log* d) SVT queries.
insights.speaker: Apple ML Research
insights.so_what: Federated privacy-preserving analytics can in principle reach central-model accuracy without a trusted curator, strengthening the on-device privacy value proposition.

insights.claim: Combined with existing shuffle-model lower bounds, the SVT result establishes an exponential separation between the SVT model and shuffle- or aggregation-based federated privacy models.

insights.so_what: Shuffle-based privacy architectures look theoretically dominated for selection-type tasks; watch for industry adoption of SVT-style primitives.
